artworks.title: Heracles, Geryon and the Slain Orthrus (Red-Figure Kylix)
artworks.description: On this Attic red-figure kylix, signed by the painter Euphronios and the potter Kachrylion, the two-headed hound Orthrus lies dead at the feet of his foes. Sprawled on the ground with both canine heads collapsed and his serpent tail trailing behind him, Orthrus has already fallen in the cattle-raid of the tenth labour: at left Heracles closes on the herd, while at right the three-bodied giant Geryon — Orthrus' master — still stands armed for the fight. The vase, found at Vulci and acquired for the Munich collection in 1831, is one of the finest archaic depictions of the watchdog of Erytheia, fixing his characteristic two heads and snake-tail. Staatliche Antikensammlungen, Munich (inv. 2620).

artworks.title: Geryon and Orthrus (Attic Black-Figure Neck-Amphora)
artworks.description: Side B of an Attic black-figure neck-amphora attributed to the Swing Painter shows the two-headed Orthrus beside his master, the three-bodied Geryon, guarding the red cattle of Erytheia. The hound is rendered in the bristling silhouette typical of archaic vase-painting, his twin heads turned toward the threat that will end him — Heracles, who in Hesiod's account slays both the watchdog and the herdsman Eurytion before driving off the herd. Made at Athens and found at Vulci, the amphora is one of the canonical sixth-century witnesses to Orthrus' two-headed form and his role as Geryon's guard-dog. Cabinet des médailles, Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris (De Ridder 223 = Luynes 715).
